originalTitle: Don’t Date Brandon review – this lazy true-crime show doesn’t start to do justice to these women’s horrors
summary: The tale of the women who came together to unpick the destructive swathe that one man cut through his local dating pool is woefully lacking in the detail you need to understand their plight. It feels voyeuristic and misguided
content: I’m beginning to suspect that the feminist movement is operating a covert psyops wing. I like to think that this is the motive force behind the slew of true-crime documentaries that show us, time and again, what bad men do and how they go about it. Perhaps the repeated stories of women – often unhappy with parts of their lives, or otherwise emotionally vulnerable – being love-bombed by apparent male saviours then finding themselves isolated, controlled, coerced, destabilised and battered into submission and sometimes killed that form the predominant subject of this popular modern genre are a way of teaching the young (especially) what is out there. Maybe it’s a way to help them spot the earliest signs of a predator’s approach and arm the innocent against them. Otherwise, you know, it’s just voyeuristic filler for the ever-gaping schedule maw. So, then, to the latest possibly instructive tool, possibly a piece of mindless rubbish: Don’t Date Brandon. It’s a strange title – both lazy and misguided, more suggestive of a 90s sitcom (ditzy roommates! Wild situations! One hot guy!) than an account of one man’s cutting of a destructive swathe through his local dating pool, which is what it is. But that is all of a piece with what is – at least on the basis of the one episode of the three that was made available for review – a lazy and misguided programme. It is based on the podcast Ex-Wives Undercover, which tells survivors’ stories about toxic relationships (gaslighters, catfishers, romance scammers, men leading double lives, those who threaten harm and those who carry it out). It is hosted by the two women around whose experiences with a man called Brandon Johnson the documentary is built. Amber Rasmussen met him online when she was 35 and became his second wife. He warned her to stay away from his ex-wife Athena Klingerman, with whom he had a four-year-old daughter Sydney, and – after he showed Amber the messages that proved Athena to be the “psycho” he said she was – Amber was happy to do so. That was until the red flags around her own relationship with Brandon – the woman claiming to be his girlfriend, the mystery job that required so much travel, the cancer diagnosis just as she was planning on moving out of the marital home, inexplicable bills and parking tickets – made her contact Athena. Whereupon they began unpicking the web of lies Brandon had been telling them both. He had of course been lying about his job, which was mostly the cover for an affair he was having with a woman called Avery (Sydney had a bedroom at her house and was told to keep everything secret from her mother and Amber), and his cancer claims (he had pretended to be ill while he was with Athena too), and about Athena’s nature. She had never run up $100,000 on his credit card, as he had told Amber, and the message threads he had shown his second wife had been completely fabricated by him over an entire year. Most of this information, however, is crammed into the last few minutes of the first episode. The rest of it is spent largely marking time. Amber outlines at length the facts of their relationship, but there is very little emphasis on the psychological effects of Brandon’s actions. Without that, the manipulation looks – to the outsider – so obvious, so blatant that you begin not to sympathise with Brandon’s victim but rather to roll your eyes at a naivety so profound. I am not saying Amber is in any way to blame, you understand. I’m saying that the programme’s pacing, and its lack of granular detail for so long, means that it does not even start to do justice to the gradual erosion of mind and spirit, the inexorable normalisation of the unacceptable, upon which perpetrators like Brandon depend. I imagine that the next two episodes concentrate on the escalation of Brandon’s behaviour (he was eventually charged with assault and attempted kidnapping with intention to commit rape, and accepted a plea agreement that means he is serving a 10-year sentence in a state prison and is eligible for parole next year) and on Amber and Athena going public with their stories. That in turn leads to the uniting of many other victims of Brandon, a man the women discover was served his first restraining order in 1997 at the age of 19. But those episodes will come on top of a shaky foundation that puts Amber (especially) and Athena in the position of effectively having something to prove about themselves, rather than about the man who hurt them. • Don’t Date Brandon is on Channel 4 now
chineseTitle: 不要和布兰登约会评论——这部懒惰的真实犯罪剧并没有开始公正地对待这些女性的恐怖
chineseSummary: 一个男人在当地的约会池中割断了破坏性的痕迹，而这些女人聚集在一起，解开这个故事，但不幸的是，这个故事缺乏了解她们困境所需的细节。感觉有偷窥和误导的感觉
chineseContent: 我开始怀疑女权运动正在运作一个秘密的心理战部门。我喜欢认为这是大量真实犯罪纪录片背后的动力，这些纪录片一次又一次地向我们展示坏人的所作所为以及他们是如何做的。也许，女性不断重复的故事——通常对自己生活的某些部分不满意，或者在情感上很脆弱——被表面上的男性救世主爱情轰炸，然后发现自己被孤立、控制、胁迫、不稳定、殴打屈服，有时甚至被杀，这些故事构成了这一流行现代流派的主要主题，是一种教导年轻人（尤其是）外面世界的方式。也许这是一种帮助它们发现掠食者接近的最早迹象并武装无辜者来对抗它们的方法。否则，你知道，这只是为了满足不断扩大的日程安排而偷窥的填充物。那么，最新的可能有启发性的工具，可能是一件愚蠢的垃圾：不要和布兰登约会。这是一个奇怪的标题——既懒惰又误导，更像是一部 90 年代的情景喜剧（愚蠢的室友！狂野的情况！一个帅哥！），而不是一个男人在他当地的约会池中切割出破坏性的一条线的描述，而事实就是如此。但这完全是一个懒惰且误导性的节目——至少从可供审查的三集中的一集来看是这样。它改编自播客《前妻卧底》，讲述了幸存者关于有毒关系的故事（煤气灯操纵者、钓鱼者、浪漫骗子、过着双重生活的男人、威胁伤害的人和实施伤害的人）。该片由两位女性主持，这部纪录片就是围绕她们与一位名叫布兰登·约翰逊的男人的经历而制作的。 Amber Rasmussen 35 岁时在网上认识了他，并成为了他的第二任妻子。他警告说
whyItMatters: 这条信息属于全球新闻信号，适合用于观察外部环境、政策变化、地缘风险和市场情绪。
